hokkaido: Japan's northernmost island, with vast farmland and seas on three sides, is a treasure trove of ingredients. Expect fresh seafood bowls, grilled lamb jingisukan and the three great ramens of Sapporo, Asahikawa and Hakodate.
aomori: At the northern tip of Honshu, Aomori grows more apples than anywhere else in Japan. Blessed with Oma tuna and scallops, it also has warming dishes like niboshi ramen and senbei-jiru to get through the snowy winters.
iwate: Japan's second-largest prefecture after Hokkaido offers food from both mountains and sea. Morioka is famous for its three noodles: reimen cold noodles, jajamen and all-you-can-eat wanko soba.
miyagi: Home to Sendai, the largest city in Tohoku, Miyagi enjoys the Sanriku coast and fertile rice fields. It is known for grilled beef tongue and sweets made with zunda, a sweet edamame paste.
akita: One of Japan's top rice regions, famous for its rice and sake. Snow country cooking shines here: kiritanpo hot pot, silky Inaniwa udon and iburigakko, smoked pickled daikon.
yamagata: A farming prefecture known for cherries, rice and premium Yonezawa beef. Locals love ramen, and the region has its own food culture, from chilled ramen to imoni taro stew.
fukushima: Divided into three regions, Aizu, Nakadori and Hamadori, each with its own climate and food. Try Kitakata and Shirakawa ramen or Aizu's sauce katsudon.
ibaraki: A major farming prefecture that feeds the Tokyo area, known for melons and sweet potatoes. Specialties include Mito natto, winter monkfish hot pot and dried sweet potato.
tochigi: Home to Nikko and Nasu and famous for its strawberries. Casual local food is a highlight, especially Utsunomiya gyoza and Sano ramen.
gunma: Wheat farming runs deep here, and so does a love of noodles and flour-based food. Try Mizusawa udon, hearty okirikomi stew and yaki manju buns glazed with sweet miso.
saitama: Right next to Tokyo, yet with a strong udon culture of its own. Simple local favorites include Musashino udon, Chichibu waraji katsudon and Gyoda's zeri fry.
chiba: Surrounded by sea on three sides, with thriving fishing and farming. Taste fishermen's namero, spicy Katsuura tantanmen and locally grown peanuts.
tokyo: Japan's food capital since the Edo period. Alongside Edo-born classics like nigiri sushi, tempura and monjayaki, you will find flavors from all over Japan and the world.
kanagawa: Home to the port of Yokohama, one of the first places in Japan to welcome Western and Chinese food. Explore Yokohama Chinatown, iekei ramen, navy curry and Shonan's raw whitebait bowls.
niigata: Japan's leading rice region, famous for Koshihikari rice and sake. It also has unique local food like tare katsudon, back-fat ramen and Niigata Italian, yakisoba topped with tomato sauce.
toyama: Facing Toyama Bay, known as a natural fish tank, it is proud of white shrimp, firefly squid and winter yellowtail. Toyama Black ramen with its jet-black soup is another specialty.
ishikawa: Centered on Kanazawa, a castle town of the wealthy Kaga domain, Ishikawa developed a refined food culture. Enjoy Sea of Japan seafood, Kanazawa oden, Kanazawa curry and traditional sweets.
fukui: Famous for Echizen crab, the king of winter flavors. Simple, addictive specialties include oroshi soba with grated daikon and sauce katsudon with thin, sauce-soaked cutlets.
yamanashi: On the north side of Mt. Fuji, Yamanashi grows more grapes and peaches than anywhere else in Japan. It is known for hoto, a hearty noodle stew, and shingen mochi with kinako and syrup.
nagano: Surrounded by high mountains, its cool climate is perfect for buckwheat. Simple mountain food lives on here: Shinshu soba, oyaki dumplings and nozawana pickles.
gifu: Combines the mountain culture of Hida-Takayama with the clear rivers of the Nagara, known for cormorant fishing. Specialties include Hida beef, hoba miso, grilled sweetfish and autumn kuri kinton.
shizuoka: Blessed with Mt. Fuji and Suruga Bay, Shizuoka has an abundance of food from mountain and sea. It is famous for green tea and wasabi, and for B-gourmet like Hamamatsu gyoza, Fujinomiya yakisoba and Shizuoka oden.
aichi: Its capital, Nagoya, is known for nagoya-meshi, a bold local food culture. Look for miso katsu, hitsumabushi eel, chicken wings and ogura toast.
mie: Home to Ise Grand Shrine, Mie has welcomed pilgrims for centuries. Nationally famous specialties include Ise lobster, Matsusaka beef, Ise udon and akafuku mochi.
shiga: Lake Biwa, Japan's largest lake, sits at its center, and a unique lake-fish cuisine grew around it. Known for fermented funazushi, Omi beef and local Omi champon noodles.
kyoto: The imperial capital for over a thousand years, Kyoto developed refined Kyoto cuisine. Enjoy seasonal flavors like yudofu, yuba, Kyoto pickles, yatsuhashi and matcha sweets.
osaka: Once called the nation's kitchen, this merchant city gave birth to the phrase kuidaore, eat until you drop. It is the home of cheap, delicious flour-based food like takoyaki, okonomiyaki and kushikatsu.
hyogo: From the port city of Kobe to areas stretching from the Sea of Japan to the Seto Inland Sea, Hyogo is full of variety. Try Kobe beef, Akashi-yaki and sobameshi.
nara: Japan's ancient capital, also famous for the deer of Nara Park. Simple, historic flavors remain, such as persimmon-leaf sushi, Miwa somen, narazuke pickles and kudzu sweets.
wakayama: In the southwest of the Kii Peninsula, Wakayama is famous for umeboshi plums and mandarin oranges. Known for rich Wakayama ramen, mehari-zushi wrapped in pickled greens and Koyasan's sesame tofu.
tottori: Home to huge sand dunes and Japan's smallest population. Enjoy ingredient-driven food such as winter snow crab, dune-grown rakkyo shallots and beef bone ramen.
shimane: The land of myths, home to Izumo Taisha shrine. Gentle, deeply flavored food includes Lake Shinji clams, dark Izumo soba and seafood from the Sea of Japan.
okayama: Called the Land of Sunshine for its mild weather, it is famous for white peaches and Muscat grapes. Specialties include kibi dango, demi-glace katsudon and kakioko oyster okonomiyaki.
hiroshima: On the Seto Inland Sea, Hiroshima produces more oysters than anywhere in Japan. Famous for layered Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, Onomichi ramen and momiji manju.
yamaguchi: At the western tip of Honshu, Shimonoseki is famous for pufferfish. You will also find dishes seen nowhere else, like kawara soba, green tea noodles served on a hot roof tile.
tokushima: Famous for the Awa Odori dance festival and for growing the most sudachi citrus in Japan. Try dark-broth Tokushima ramen topped with a raw egg and Iya soba from the mountain villages.
kagawa: Japan's smallest prefecture calls itself the Udon Prefecture, and Sanuki udon is part of daily life. There are countless udon shops, and honetsukidori chicken is another favorite.
ehime: Facing the Seto Inland Sea and the Uwa Sea, Ehime is known for citrus and red sea bream. Seafood dishes abound, including two styles of taimeshi, jakoten fish cakes and Imabari's roast pork and egg rice.
kochi: Facing the Pacific and known for bonito fishing. Its bold food culture includes straw-seared katsuo no tataki and sawachi ryori, a feast served on large platters.
fukuoka: Home to Fukuoka City, the largest city in Kyushu, and its famous yatai food stalls. The center of Kyushu food: tonkotsu Hakata ramen, motsunabe, mizutaki and spicy mentaiko.
saga: Faces two seas, the Ariake Sea and the Genkai Sea. It is full of hidden gems, such as Saga beef, ultra-fresh Yobuko squid and the melting tofu of Ureshino Onsen.
nagasaki: As Japan's window to the world during the Edo period, Nagasaki developed food influenced by China and Portugal. Famous for champon, sara udon, castella cake and Turkish rice.
kumamoto: Blessed with the dramatic nature of Mt. Aso and abundant water. Distinctive specialties include basashi horse sashimi, karashi renkon, Kumamoto ramen with burnt garlic oil and akaushi beef.
oita: The Onsen Prefecture, with more hot springs and hot spring water than anywhere in Japan. Try jigoku mushi steamed in hot spring vapor, toriten, Nakatsu karaage and premium Seki aji and Seki saba.
miyazaki: A warm climate makes it famous for mangoes, Miyazaki beef and free-range chicken. Bold southern flavors include chicken nanban, hiyajiru cold soup and spicy karamen.
kagoshima: Southern Kyushu's prefecture, watched over by the Sakurajima volcano, is famous for black pork, shochu and sweet potatoes. Try black pork tonkatsu or shabu-shabu, shirokuma shaved ice and keihan chicken rice.
okinawa: Once the Ryukyu Kingdom, Okinawa developed a food culture different from mainland Japan. Okinawa soba, goya champuru, taco rice and sata andagi doughnuts are favorites.
